new_statements.quote: [p. 46, Summary] The Ikema dialect of Miyako, Southern Ryukyuan, has a three-pattern accent system in which three tone classes (Types A, B, and C) are lexically contrastive, although the Type A simplex nouns are fewer. [p. 46] 池間方言は，語の長さが増えてもアクセント型の対立数が増加せず，その対立数が 3 である三型アクセント体系（上野 1984, 2012）を有する。[...] 三型アクセント体系を有する宮古語諸方言には，池間方言のほかに，多良間方言（松森 2010），与那覇方言（松森 2013），狩俣方言（松森 2015）がある [p. 50] 非中和環境において，2 番目の韻律語と 3 番目の韻律語の双方に高ピッチが現れない型を A 型，2 番目の韻律語に高ピッチが現れず 3 番目の韻律語に高ピッチが現れる型を B 型，2 番目の韻律語に高ピッチが現れるが 3 番目の韻律語に高ピッチが現れない型を C 型と定義し，議論を進める。
new_statements.translation: [p. 46] The Ikema dialect does not increase its number of contrasting accent types as words get longer; it has a three-pattern accent system (Uwano 1984, 2012) with three contrasts. [...] Besides Ikema, the Miyako dialects with a three-pattern accent system include Tarama (Matsumori 2010), Yonaha (Matsumori 2013) and Karimata (Matsumori 2015). [p. 50] In non-neutralizing environments we define as Type A the pattern in which high pitch appears on neither the second nor the third prosodic word, as Type B the pattern in which high pitch does not appear on the second prosodic word but does on the third, and as Type C the pattern in which high pitch appears on the second prosodic word but not on the third, and proceed on that basis.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word stress is described. Ikema Miyako has a three-way lexically contrastive tone-class (N-pattern 'accent') system: every noun belongs to Type A, B or C, and the class is realized as a distribution of high pitch over prosodic words in the phrase, not at a fixed position in the word. Prosodic words are built by rule (1), p. 47: 'insert a prosodic-word boundary at the left edge of every root or clitic of two or more moras' (one-mora clitics fuse with the preceding prosodic word). The three-way contrast is neutralized in most short environments and surfaces only when the phrase contains three (or more) prosodic words or is followed by a predicate; Type A high pitch falls on neither the 2nd nor the 3rd prosodic word, Type B on the 3rd, Type C on the 2nd. Type A simplex nouns are rare (about 5%, 6 of 121 nouns) because of a historical merger of A into B.
new_statements.exceptions: 4-mora simplex nouns keep the three-way contrast even in a two-prosodic-word phrase (5b, p. 50); older descriptions (Hirayama 1964, 1983; Hirayama et al. 1967; Sakimura 2006; Hayashi et al. 2008) wrongly gave Ikema a two-pattern system (p. 46); speakers tend to put phonetic prominence on an utterance-final clitic (especially =mai), which obscures the accent contrast (pp. 50-51); Type A nouns that share particular meanings (numbers, people, time, space, place names) resisted the A>B merger (sec. 3-4).
new_statements.identity_note: Work 1's substitute (Igarashi 2016) describes the Ikema dialect of Miyako, with all data recorded in the Nishihara settlement of Miyakojima (Ikema is spoken on Ikema island, in Sarahama on Irabu, and in Nishihara on Miyakojima), p. 46. Work 0 concerns Tarama (Tarama island), a distinct Miyako variety, not opened. The statement that Tarama, Yonaha and Karimata are also three-pattern systems is Igarashi's citation of Matsumori, not a direct reading of those sources. Earlier on-disk files in the same directory (Shimoji 2009 on Irabu, Pellard 2009 on Ogami, Igarashi et al. 2012 on Ikema) were downloaded by an earlier reading and were not in this task's works list, so they were not re-read here.

tone_statements.translation: [p.85] From these facts it has become clear that the Yonaha dialect is a 'three-pattern system' consisting of three tonal patterns (LLH, LHL, HLL). ... [p.87] That is, in Yonaha the tonal melodies LLH for Type A, LHL for Type B and HLL for Type C must be taken to be specified item by item in the lexicon. We have also seen that, while the 'three patterns' hardly become visible with simplex words, the three-way distinction stands out sharply once compounds are used. ... [p.67, abstract] a constraint is involved whereby 'three morae form one unit, a foot, and the H tone is realised on that foot'.

readall_conflicts: Within the literature that source reports, there is a historical conflict: Hirayama (1964, 1983), Hirayama et al. (1967), Sakimura (2006) and Hayashi et al. (2008) described Ikema (and the other Miyako dialects) as two-pattern accent systems, which Igarashi (2016, p. 46) calls an error caused by widespread neutralization and by the near-absence of Type A simplex nouns; Igarashi et al. (2011a, 2012) and Matsumori (2010, 2013, 2015) establish three patterns for Ikema, Tarama, Yonaha and Karimata. The Brill 2026 Tarama and Ikema chapters could not be opened, so whether they add stress-related statements remains unknown.

sources.note: Ikema and Tarama both have a 'three-pattern accent system' with three lexically contrastive accentual classes; the three-way contrast is neutralised in a wide range of contexts and the realisation rules are more complex than in Japanese dialects; argues both systems can only be described by positing a Prosodic Word onto which polymoraic roots and clitics are mapped, and discusses whether that category is properly the Prosodic Word. Not downloaded (one-download option used on work 1).

sources.note: Treats the Irabu dialect as an accentless (無アクセント) dialect and analyses its intonation against modality, syntactic branching and focus: the basic unit is a 'へ'-shaped pitch contour repeated per accentual phrase (phrase-initial rise) inside intonation phrases; modality is marked at the IP right edge, questions by a sharp fall and overall high pitch; focus adds a prominence on the phrase-final particle plus pause but no pitch-range expansion or compression. I.e. states no lexical accent, consistent with Shimoji 2008/2009. Not downloaded.
